topic_title: Computer Networks: L3 - Ethernet Framing, ARP & IPv4 Subnetting
learning_objectives: Dissect the exact structure of an Ethernet II frame and explain the physical necessity of the 64-byte minimum frame size.
Master the switch MAC learning algorithm and distinguish switch CAM tables from host ARP tables.
Explain the Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) workflow, frame formats, and security implications.
Understand Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU) constraints and calculate IP packet fragmentation parameters.
Convert 32-bit IPv4 addresses between binary bitstreams and dotted-decimal notation effortlessly.
Apply subnet masks via bitwise ANDing to determine Network ID, Broadcast ID, and usable host capacity using 2^H - 2.
Differentiate Classful addressing from Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) and identify RFC 1918 private ranges.
Trace the complete Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) 4-step DORA handshake.
summary: In-depth lecture notes for Lecture 3: Layer 2 Ethernet, ARP & Layer 3 IPv4 Subnetting, covering theoretical foundations, mathematical formulations, protocol packet traces, and hands-on CLI verification.
key_takeaways: Ethernet II frames require a minimum payload of 46 bytes to satisfy the 64-byte minimum frame size mandated by CSMA/CD slot time physics.
Switches learn Source MACs on inbound ports; ARP maps IP addresses to MAC addresses via broadcast requests and unicast replies.
Subnet masks split 32-bit IPv4 addresses into Network ID and Host ID via bitwise AND; usable hosts = 2^H - 2.
IP fragmentation divides packets exceeding link MTU (1500 B) using Identification, Flags (DF, MF), and 8-byte Fragment Offsets.
DHCP leases IP addresses via 4 steps (DORA): Discover (Broadcast) -> Offer (Unicast/Broadcast) -> Request (Broadcast) -> Acknowledge (Unicast).

sections.heading: 1. Layer 2 Ethernet II Frame Anatomy & The 64-Byte Physics
sections.body:
### Ethernet II Frame Anatomy
The standard framing protocol of the global Internet LAN is **Ethernet II** (DIX standard):

```text
┌──────────────┬─────┬─────────────┬─────────────┬───────────┬────────────────────┬───────────┐
│   Preamble   │ SFD │  Dest MAC   │ Source MAC  │ EtherType │      Payload       │  FCS/CRC  │
│    7 Bytes   │ 1 B │   6 Bytes   │   6 Bytes   │  2 Bytes  │   46 - 1500 Bytes  │  4 Bytes  │
└──────────────┴─────┴─────────────┴─────────────┴───────────┴────────────────────┴───────────┘
 ◄──────── Physical Preamble ────────►◄────────────────── MAC Frame (64 - 1518 Bytes) ────────►
```

1. **Preamble (7 Bytes)**: Repeating alternating bit pattern `10101010` used by the physical receiver's clock recovery circuit to synchronize bit timing.
2. **Start Frame Delimiter / SFD (1 Byte)**: The sequence `10101011`, indicating that the very next bit is the start of the destination MAC address.
3. **Destination MAC (6 Bytes / 48 bits)**: Physical hardware address of the receiving interface or broadcast `ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff`.
4. **Source MAC (6 Bytes / 48 bits)**: Physical hardware address of the transmitting network interface.
5. **EtherType (2 Bytes)**: Identifies the encapsulated Layer 3 protocol:
   - `0x0800`: IPv4
   - `0x0806`: Address Resolution Protocol (ARP)
   - `0x86DD`: IPv6
6. **Payload (46 to 1500 Bytes)**: The encapsulated Layer 3 packet.
7. **Frame Check Sequence / FCS (4 Bytes)**: A 32-bit Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC-32) calculated over MAC addresses, EtherType, and payload. If the receiver's computed CRC does not match, the corrupted frame is silently dropped.

### The Physics of the 64-Byte Minimum Frame Size
In standard Ethernet (IEEE 802.3), the minimum frame size is **64 bytes** ($6 + 6 + 2 + 46 + 4 = 64$). If the payload is smaller than 46 bytes, padding bytes (`0x00`) are inserted.

Why 64 bytes?
In classic half-duplex Ethernet, devices shared a bus using **CSMA/CD (Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection)**:
1. Suppose Node A and Node B are separated by maximum allowed cable segment distance $d_{\text{max}}$.
2. Node A begins transmitting. Just before Node A's first bit reaches Node B at propagation delay $\tau$, Node B senses an idle line and transmits.
3. A collision occurs immediately near Node B. The collision signal must now travel back to Node A across the cable, taking another $\tau$ seconds.
4. Total round-trip collision detection time is **$2\tau$** (the **Slot Time**).
5. For Node A to detect the collision while it is still actively transmitting, the transmission delay $d_{\text{trans}}$ must exceed the slot time:
   $$d_{\text{trans}} = \frac{L_{\text{min}}}{R} \ge 2\tau$$
6. In original $10\text{ Mbps}$ Ethernet, slot time was standardized to $51.2\ \mu\text{s}$:
   $$L_{\text{min}} = 10\text{ Mbps} \times 51.2\ \mu\text{s} = 512\text{ bits} = 64\text{ Bytes}$$

Frames smaller than 64 bytes are known as **runt frames** and are discarded as transmission collisions by network interfaces.
citations: Kurose & Ross, Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach, Chapter 6.4

sections.heading: 2. Switch MAC Learning & The CAM Table
sections.body:
### How Layer 2 Switches Operate Unlike dumb hubs that blindly broadcast signals out all ports, an Ethernet switch maintains a **Content Addressable Memory (CAM) Table** mapping MAC addresses to physical ports: ```mermaid sequenceDiagram autonumber participant HostA as Host A (Port 1) participant Switch as Layer 2 Switch participant HostB as Host B (Port 2) participant HostC as Host C (Port 3) HostA->>Switch: 1. Sends frame with Src=MAC_A, Dst=MAC_B Note over Switch: Switch inspects Src=MAC_A on Port 1:
Learns (MAC_A -> Port 1) Note over Switch: Dst=MAC_B not in CAM table! -> Unknown Unicast Flooding Switch->>HostB: Floods copy out Port 2 Switch->>HostC: Floods copy out Port 3 HostC-->>Switch: Ignores (Dst MAC mismatch) HostB->>Switch: 2. Host B replies: Src=MAC_B, Dst=MAC_A Note over Switch: Switch learns (MAC_B -> Port 2).
Dst=MAC_A is known on Port 1 -> Unicast forwarding! Switch->>HostA: Forwards directly out Port 1 only ``` ### The Three Forwarding Rules of an Ethernet Switch 1. **Learn**: Examine the **Source MAC** of every inbound frame and associate it with the ingress port in the CAM table with an aging timer (typically 300 seconds). 2. **Forward**: If the **Destination MAC** is already recorded in the CAM table, forward the frame *only* out the corresponding port. 3. **Flood**: If the Destination MAC is unknown (Unknown Unicast) or is the broadcast address (`ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff`), copy and flood the frame out *all* ports except the port on which it arrived.

sections.heading: 3. Address Resolution Protocol (ARP)
sections.body:
### Bridging Layer 3 IP to Layer 2 MAC When Host A wants to send an IP packet to Host B on the same local subnet, it knows Host B's destination IP address, but its network card cannot construct an Ethernet frame without Host B's hardware MAC address. **ARP (Address Resolution Protocol)** dynamically discovers this mapping: ```mermaid sequenceDiagram autonumber participant HostA as Host A
(192.168.1.10) participant Switch as L2 Switch participant HostB as Host B
(192.168.1.20) Note over HostA: ARP Cache miss for 192.168.1.20 HostA->>Switch: 1. ARP Request (Broadcast: ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff)
"Who has 192.168.1.20? Tell 192.168.1.10" Switch->>HostB: Floods broadcast to all ports Note over HostB: Matches own IP! Updates ARP cache with (192.168.1.10 -> MAC_A) HostB->>Switch: 2. ARP Reply (Unicast to MAC_A)
"192.168.1.20 is at MAC_B" Switch->>HostA: Forwards unicast directly to Port 1 Note over HostA: Host A caches (192.168.1.20 -> MAC_B).
Now transmits pending IP data frame! ``` > [!IMPORTANT] > **ARP Table vs. Switch MAC (CAM) Table**: > - **ARP Table (Host OS)**: Maps **IP Address $\to$ MAC Address** (e.g., `192.168.1.20 -> aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff`). Resides in the host operating system memory. View via `arp -a`. > - **MAC / CAM Table (Switch)**: Maps **MAC Address $\to$ Physical Port** (e.g., `aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff -> Port FastEthernet 0/2`). Resides inside switch hardware ASIC memory. View on Cisco via `show mac address-table`. ### ARP Spoofing / Poisoning Vulnerability Because standard ARP has no authentication, any malicious machine on the LAN can emit unsolicited ARP replies claiming to own the default gateway's IP address. Switches and hosts naively accept these replies, enabling Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) packet interception.
citations: RFC 826 - An Ethernet Address Resolution Protocol

sections.heading: 4. Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU) & IP Fragmentation
sections.body:
### Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU)
The **Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU)** is the maximum payload size (in bytes) that a Layer 2 frame can carry:
- **Standard Ethernet MTU**: $1500\text{ Bytes}$.
- **Jumbo Frames**: Up to $9000\text{ Bytes}$ (used in data center storage fabrics).

### IP Packet Fragmentation
When a Layer 3 router receives a packet larger than the MTU of its outgoing interface, it must divide the packet into smaller fragments:

```text
ORIGINAL IP PACKET (4200 Bytes Total = 20B Header + 4180B Payload)
Incoming Interface MTU: 9000 Bytes  ────►  Outgoing Link MTU: 1500 Bytes
                                            (Max data payload = 1500 - 20 = 1480B)

FRAGMENT 1:
Length: 1500 B (20B Header + 1480B Data) | MF = 1 | Offset = 0
FRAGMENT 2:
Length: 1500 B (20B Header + 1480B Data) | MF = 1 | Offset = 1480 / 8 = 185
FRAGMENT 3:
Length: 1240 B (20B Header + 1220B Data) | MF = 0 | Offset = 2960 / 8 = 370
```

1. **Identification (16 bits)**: Copied identically to all fragments so the destination host knows which fragments belong together.
2. **Flags (3 bits)**:
   - **DF (Don't Fragment)**: If set to `1` and the packet exceeds link MTU, the router drops the packet and sends an ICMP Type 3 Code 4 error ("Fragmentation Needed but DF set"). This powers **Path MTU Discovery (PMTUD)**.
   - **MF (More Fragments)**: Set to `1` for all fragments except the final fragment (`MF = 0`).
3. **Fragment Offset (13 bits)**: Specifies the position of this fragment's data relative to the beginning of the original packet, measured in **units of 8-byte blocks** ($1480 / 8 = 185$).

Fragments are **never** reassembled by intermediate routers; reassembly occurs solely at the final destination host's kernel stack.

sections.heading: 5. IPv4 Architecture & Binary Conversion Masterclass
sections.body:
### IPv4 Format Fundamentals
An IPv4 address is an unsigned **32-bit integer**, written as four decimal octets separated by periods:
```text
      192     .     168     .      1      .      5
   [Octet 1]     [Octet 2]     [Octet 3]     [Octet 4]
    8 bits        8 bits        8 bits        8 bits   = 32 bits total
```
Total address space: $2^{32} = 4,294,967,296 \approx 4.3\text{ billion addresses}$.

### 8-Bit Powers of Two Reference Table
Every 8-bit octet is constructed from the sum of powers of 2:
| Bit Position | 7 | 6 | 5 | 4 | 3 | 2 | 1 | 0 |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Decimal Weight** | **128** | **64** | **32** | **16** | **8** | **4** | **2** | **1** |

### Step-by-Step Conversion Algorithm

#### Decimal to Binary Example: 192
- Is $192 \ge 128$? Yes $\to$ **1**, remainder $= 192 - 128 = 64$.
- Is $64 \ge 64$? Yes $\to$ **1**, remainder $= 64 - 64 = 0$.
- Remaining positions are all **0**.
$$\mathbf{192} = 11000000_2$$

#### Decimal to Binary Example: 168
- $168 \ge 128$ $\to$ **1**, remainder $= 40$.
- $40 < 64$ $\to$ **0**.
- $40 \ge 32$ $\to$ **1**, remainder $= 8$.
- $8 < 16$ $\to$ **0**.
- $8 \ge 8$ $\to$ **1**, remainder $= 0$.
$$\mathbf{168} = 10101000_2$$

$$\mathbf{192.168.1.5} = \mathbf{11000000.10101000.00000001.00000101_2}$$

sections.heading: 6. Subnet Masks, Network IDs & CIDR Calculations
sections.body:
### Anatomy of an IP Address: Network Portion vs. Host Portion
Every IP address consists of two structural parts:
1. **Network ID**: Identifies the specific network segment (analogous to a postal ZIP code).
2. **Host ID**: Identifies the specific endpoint on that network (analogous to a house number).

### The Subnet Mask Bitwise AND Operation
A **Subnet Mask** is a 32-bit sequence of consecutive `1`s followed by consecutive `0`s. Routers compute the Network ID using bitwise **AND**:

$$\text{Network ID} = \text{IP Address} \mathbin{\&} \text{Subnet Mask}$$

```text
IP Address:   192.168.  1.  5   ->  11000000.10101000.00000001.00000101
Subnet Mask:  255.255.255.  0   ->  11111111.11111111.11111111.00000000
------------------------------------------------------------------------
Bitwise AND:  192.168.  1.  0   ->  11000000.10101000.00000001.00000000 (Network ID)
```

### The Usable Host Formula: $2^H - 2$
For a subnet with $H$ host bits:
$$\text{Total IP Addresses} = 2^H$$
$$\text{Usable Hosts} = 2^H - 2$$

Why subtract 2?
1. **Network Address (All Host Bits = 0)**: Identifies the network itself (e.g., `192.168.1.0`). Cannot be assigned to a host.
2. **Directed Broadcast Address (All Host Bits = 1)**: Sends packets to every host on that subnet (e.g., `192.168.1.255`).

### Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR)
Before 1993, addresses were divided into rigid, wasteful classes:
- **Class A**: Leading `0`, `/8`, 16 million hosts per network.
- **Class B**: Leading `10`, `/16`, 65,534 hosts per network.
- **Class C**: Leading `110`, `/24`, 254 hosts per network.

**CIDR (RFC 1519)** abolished classes, allowing arbitrary prefix lengths (`/N` notation):
- `/24`: 24 network bits, 8 host bits $\to 2^8 - 2 = 254$ usable hosts.
- `/25`: 25 network bits, 7 host bits $\to 2^7 - 2 = 126$ usable hosts.
- `/26`: 26 network bits, 6 host bits $\to 2^6 - 2 = 62$ usable hosts.
- `/27`: 27 network bits, 5 host bits $\to 2^5 - 2 = 30$ usable hosts.
- `/28`: 28 network bits, 4 host bits $\to 2^4 - 2 = 14$ usable hosts.
- `/30`: 30 network bits, 2 host bits $\to 2^2 - 2 = 2$ usable hosts (used for point-to-point router links).
citations: RFC 4632 - Classless Inter-domain Routing (CIDR): The Internet Address Assignment and Aggregation Plan

sections.heading: 7. RFC 1918 Private Ranges & Special Reserved Addresses
sections.body:
### Private IP Address Ranges (RFC 1918)
To conserve IPv4 addresses, RFC 1918 reserved three non-routable address blocks for internal LANs:

| Class Block | CIDR Prefix | IP Address Range | Total Available Addresses | Common Deployment Use-Case |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Class A Private** | `10.0.0.0/8` | `10.0.0.0` - `10.255.255.255` | 16,777,216 | Large enterprise networks & AWS VPCs |
| **Class B Private** | `172.16.0.0/12` | `172.16.0.0` - `172.31.255.255` | 1,048,576 | Mid-size university campus networks |
| **Class C Private** | `192.168.0.0/16` | `192.168.0.0` - `192.168.255.255` | 65,536 | Home routers & small office Wi-Fi LANs |

> [!WARNING]
> Private addresses are **dropped by Internet routers**. Devices in private subnets communicate with the public internet exclusively via **Network Address Translation (NAT)** on the perimeter gateway router.

### Special Reserved IPv4 Addresses
- `0.0.0.0/32`: "This host on this network" (used as source address by DHCP clients before receiving an IP).
- `0.0.0.0/0`: The **Default Route** in routing tables (matches all unmatched destinations).
- `127.0.0.1/8`: **Loopback Interface** (`localhost`). Packets never reach a physical NIC; they are routed internally inside the OS kernel.
- `169.254.0.0/16`: **APIPA (Automatic Private IP Addressing)**. Self-assigned by Windows/macOS when DHCP server fails to respond.
- `255.255.255.255`: **Limited Broadcast**. Flooded to all local LAN devices, never forwarded across routers.
citations: RFC 1918 - Address Allocation for Private Internets

sections.heading: 8. Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) & The DORA Flow
sections.body:
### Automated IP Configuration via DORA Instead of manually typing static IP addresses, clients use **DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol)** running over UDP (Port 67 on server, Port 68 on client): ```mermaid sequenceDiagram autonumber participant Client as New Client Host
(0.0.0.0, Port 68) participant Switch as L2 Switch participant DHCP as DHCP Server
(192.168.1.1, Port 67) Note over Client: Step 1: DISCOVER Client->>Switch: DHCP Discover (UDP Broadcast: 255.255.255.255)
Src IP: 0.0.0.0, Dst IP: 255.255.255.255 Switch->>DHCP: Floods broadcast to DHCP Server Note over DHCP: Step 2: OFFER DHCP->>Switch: DHCP Offer
Offered IP: 192.168.1.50, Mask: /24, Gateway: 192.168.1.1, DNS: 8.8.8.8 Switch->>Client: Forwards Offer to Client Note over Client: Step 3: REQUEST Client->>Switch: DHCP Request (Broadcast)
"I accept lease for 192.168.1.50 from DHCP Server 192.168.1.1" Switch->>DHCP: Delivers Request to Server Note over DHCP: Step 4: ACKNOWLEDGE DHCP->>Switch: DHCP ACK
Confirms lease duration (e.g. 86400s) and commits IP assignment Switch->>Client: Client sets IP to 192.168.1.50! ``` 1. **Discover (Client $\to$ All)**: Broadcasts asking if any DHCP server is present on the segment. 2. **Offer (Server $\to$ Client)**: Server reserves an available IP and offers it along with Subnet Mask, Default Gateway, DNS servers, and Lease Time. 3. **Request (Client $\to$ All)**: Broadcasts formal acceptance. (Broadcast so other DHCP servers know their offers were declined and can release reserved IPs). 4. **Acknowledge / ACK (Server $\to$ Client)**: Server confirms the binding and commits the lease duration.
citations: RFC 2132 - DHCP Options and BOOTP Vendor Extensions

sections.heading: 9. Synthesis: Complete Hop-by-Hop Trace & CLI Diagnostics
sections.body:
### Putting It All Together: A Hop-by-Hop Packet Trace
When Host A (`192.168.1.10`) pings an external server (`8.8.8.8`):
1. **Subnet Mask Check**: Host A computes `8.8.8.8 & 255.255.255.0 = 8.8.8.0 != 192.168.1.0`. Host A recognizes destination is on a **remote network**.
2. **Default Gateway Resolution**: Host A must forward the packet to its Default Gateway (`192.168.1.1`).
3. **ARP Check**: Host A checks local ARP table for `192.168.1.1`. If missing, it emits an ARP Request broadcast (`ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff`) and caches the Gateway's MAC (`MAC_GW`).
4. **Frame Assembly**:
   - Layer 3 IP Header: $\text{Src IP} = 192.168.1.10$, $\text{Dst IP} = 8.8.8.8$, $\text{TTL} = 64$.
   - Layer 2 Ethernet Header: $\text{Src MAC} = \text{MAC}_A$, $\text{Dst MAC} = \text{MAC}_{\text{GW}}$, $\text{EtherType} = 0x0800$.
5. **Gateway Processing**:
   - Default Gateway strips L2 frame, validates IP checksum, decrements TTL to 63.
   - Looks up `8.8.8.8` in WAN routing table, finds next-hop ISP router, and re-encapsulates the IP packet into a new WAN L2 frame.

### Diagnostic Verification Commands
```bash
# Display ARP table entries
arp -a
# On modern Linux:
ip neighbor show

# Display assigned IP and subnet mask
ip addr show
# On Windows PowerShell:
Get-NetIPAddress | Format-Table

# View system routing table and default gateway
ip route show
route print
```
citations: W. Richard Stevens, TCP/IP Illustrated, Volume 1: The Protocols

heading: 8. RFC 1918 Private Addressing, Loopback & Network Address Translation (NAT)
body:
### Public vs. Private IPv4 Addresses Because the 32-bit IPv4 pool is limited to 4.3 billion addresses, not every laptop, phone, and smart lightbulb on Earth can hold a globally unique public IP. In 1996, **RFC 1918** reserved three distinct IP address blocks strictly for internal local area networks: ### The Three RFC 1918 Private Address Ranges | Class Block | CIDR Prefix | Subnet Mask | IP Address Range | Total Addresses | Typical Deployment Scenario | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **Class A Private** | **`10.0.0.0/8`** | `255.0.0.0` | `10.0.0.0` – `10.255.255.255` | **16,777,216** | Large enterprise campuses & AWS/GCP cloud VPCs | | **Class B Private** | **`172.16.0.0/12`** | `255.240.0.0` | `172.16.0.0` – `172.31.255.255` | **1,048,576** | Medium-size corporate networks & universities | | **Class C Private** | **`192.168.0.0/16`** | `255.255.0.0` | `192.168.0.0` – `192.168.255.255` | **65,536** | Home broadband routers & small business Wi-Fi | > [!WARNING] > **Private IP Addresses are NEVER Routed on the Public Internet**: > Core Internet routers are explicitly configured to drop all incoming packets with destination addresses inside RFC 1918 private ranges. Private IPs can be reused independently inside millions of private homes without conflict! --- ### Special Reserved IPv4 Addresses - **`0.0.0.0/32`**: Represents "this host on this network" (used as temporary source IP by DHCP clients before receiving an assignment). - **`0.0.0.0/0`**: The **Default Route** in routing tables (matches all traffic that has no specific subnet route). - **`127.0.0.0/8` (Loopback)**: The entire `/8` block is reserved for host internal loopback. Most commonly `127.0.0.1` (`localhost`). Packets never reach a physical NIC; they loop back internally inside the OS network stack. - **`169.254.0.0/16` (APIPA)**: *Automatic Private IP Addressing*. Self-assigned by Windows/macOS when a DHCP server fails to respond. - **`255.255.255.255`**: *Limited Broadcast*. Flooded across the local LAN segment; dropped by routers. --- ### How a Device Decides: Direct Local Delivery or Default Gateway? When a host prepares to transmit an IP packet, it determines whether the destination is local or remote by performing a bitwise AND comparison: ```text Is Local = (Local_IP & Local_Subnet_Mask) == (Dest_IP & Local_Subnet_Mask) ``` - **If Equal (Local Destination)**: The target is on the same physical subnet. The host emits an ARP request directly for the target host's IP and sends the frame straight to the target's MAC. - **If Not Equal (Remote Destination)**: The target resides on an external network. The host **does NOT ARP for the destination IP**; it looks up its **Default Gateway IP** (its local router interface), ARPs for the Default Gateway's MAC, and forwards the frame to the router! --- ### Network Address Translation (NAT) & Port Address Translation (PAT) How do thousands of workstations with private IPs (e.g., `192.168.1.X`) communicate with public servers on the Internet? Via **Network Address Translation (NAT / PAT - RFC 3022)** running on the border router: ```mermaid sequenceDiagram autonumber participant Client as Private Host
(192.168.1.50) participant NAT as Gateway Router (NAT)
(LAN: 192.168.1.1
WAN: 203.0.113.1) participant Server as Public Web Server
(93.184.216.34:80) Note over Client: Emits outbound HTTP packet
Src: 192.168.1.50:52110
Dst: 93.184.216.34:80 Client->>NAT: Sends packet to Default Gateway Note over NAT: 1. Rewrites Source IP: 203.0.113.1
2. Allocates Public Port: 10045
3. Logs in NAT State Table:
[192.168.1.50:52110 <-> 203.0.113.1:10045] NAT->>Server: Transmits translated packet over Internet Note over Server: Sees request from 203.0.113.1:10045
Generates HTTP Response! Server->>NAT: Response: Dst 203.0.113.1:10045 Note over NAT: Consults NAT Table:
Port 10045 -> 192.168.1.50:52110
Rewrites Dest IP and Port! NAT->>Client: Delivers packet to internal private client! ``` **Port Address Translation (PAT / NAT Overload)** allows thousands of internal hosts to simultaneously share a single public IP by tracking ephemeral 16-bit TCP/UDP port allocations in an internal state table.
citations: RFC 1918 - Address Allocation for Private Internets (1996)
RFC 3022 - Traditional IP Network Address Translator (Traditional NAT)
Kurose & Ross, Section 4.3.4: Network Address Translation (NAT)

citations.heading: 9. DHCP Handshake (DORA) & IPv6 Modern Transition
citations.body:
### Automated Host Configuration: The DHCP Protocol
Typing static IP addresses, subnet masks, default gateways, and DNS resolvers manually onto every smartphone and laptop is unmanageable.
The **Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP - RFC 2131)** automates host network configuration via a 4-step sequence running over UDP (Server listens on Port 67, Client listens on Port 68), remembered by the acronym **DORA**:

```text
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                       THE 4-STEP DHCP DORA SEQUENCE                         │
│                                                                             │
│  [1. DISCOVER]  Client (0.0.0.0:68) ──► (Broadcast 255.255.255.255:67)     │
│                 "Is there any DHCP server on this LAN?"                     │
│                                                                             │
│  [2. OFFER]     DHCP Server ──► Client                                      │
│                 "Here is an available IP: 192.168.1.50, Mask: /24,          │
│                  Gateway: 192.168.1.1, DNS: 8.8.8.8, Lease: 86400s"         │
│                                                                             │
│  [3. REQUEST]   Client ──► (Broadcast 255.255.255.255:67)                  │
│                 "I formally accept the offer from DHCP Server 192.168.1.1!" │
│                                                                             │
│  [4. ACK]       DHCP Server ──► Client                                      │
│                 "Lease confirmed for 24 hours. Configuration committed!"    │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

1. **Discover**: Client broadcasts on the local LAN because it does not yet have an IP address.
2. **Offer**: DHCP server reserves an available IP from its pool and sends back an offer containing IP, Mask, Gateway, DNS, and Lease Time.
3. **Request**: Client broadcasts formal acceptance (broadcast so other DHCP servers know their offers were declined and can release reserved IPs).
4. **Acknowledge (ACK)**: Server commits the binding and starts the lease countdown.

---

### The Next Generation: IPv6 Architecture
In 2011, the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) officially exhausted its primary pool of unallocated IPv4 address blocks. The long-term architectural solution is **IPv6 (RFC 8200)**:
- **Bit Length**: **128 bits (16 Bytes)**.
- **Address Space Capacity**:
  $$2^{128} = 340,282,366,920,938,463,463,374,607,431,768,211,456 \approx 3.4 \times 10^{38}\text{ addresses}$$
  *(Enough to assign billions of unique IP addresses to every grain of sand on Earth!)*
- **Format**: Written as **8 groups of 4 hexadecimal digits** separated by colons:
  `2001:0db8:85a3:0000:0000:8a2e:0370:7334`

### IPv6 Address Compression Rules
To make 128-bit addresses readable, RFC 4291 defines two strict rules:
1. **Omit Leading Zeros**: Within any 4-digit hexadecimal group, leading zeros can be omitted:
   `0db8` $\to$ `db8`, `0000` $\to$ `0`, `0370` $\to$ `370`.
   Result: `2001:db8:85a3:0:0:8a2e:370:7334`.
2. **Double Colon (`::`) Zero Compression**: A single contiguous sequence of one or more all-zero groups can be compressed into a double colon `::`:
   `2001:db8:85a3::8a2e:370:7334`.
   *(Crucial Rule: `::` can appear **only once** in an address to avoid mathematical ambiguity).*

### Common Standard IPv6 Addresses
| IPv6 Address | Classification & Purpose | IPv4 Equivalent |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `::1` | **Loopback Interface** (`localhost`) | `127.0.0.1` |
| `::` | **Unspecified Address** (all zeros) | `0.0.0.0` |
| `fe80::/10` | **Link-Local Address** (auto-configured on every NIC, valid only on local link) | APIPA (`169.254.X.X`) |
| `ff00::/8` | **Multicast Address Block** | `224.0.0.0/4` |
| `2000::/3` | **Global Unicast** (publicly routable Internet addresses) | Public IPv4 |

### Head-to-Head Architectural Comparison: IPv4 vs. IPv6
| Architectural Feature | IPv4 | IPv6 |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Address Length** | 32 bits (4 bytes) | 128 bits (16 bytes) |
| **Address Representation** | Dotted-decimal (`192.168.1.1`) | Hexadecimal colon (`2001:db8::1`) |
| **Total Address Pool** | $\approx 4.3 \times 10^9$ | $\approx 3.4 \times 10^{38}$ |
| **Header Length** | Variable (20 – 60 bytes) | Fixed (strictly 40 bytes) |
| **Broadcast Support** | Native broadcast (`255.255.255.255`) | **No broadcast** (eliminated in favor of multicast) |
| **Address Resolution** | ARP (broadcast-based) | **NDP (Neighbor Discovery Protocol)** via ICMPv6 multicast |
| **NAT Necessity** | Mandatory due to address exhaustion | Unnecessary (end-to-end addressing restored) |
| **Router Fragmentation** | Intermediate routers fragment packets | **Routers never fragment**; sender must do PMTUD |
| **Auto-Configuration** | Requires DHCP server | **SLAAC (Stateless Address Autoconfiguration)** |
citations: RFC 8200 - Internet Protocol, Version 6 (IPv6) Specification (Internet Standard, 2017)
